extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset that addresses three core research problems in scene understanding: detecting non-iconic views of objects, contextual reasoning between objects and the precise 2D localization of objects.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Images were collected by querying for pairs of objects or scene/object category pairs to find non-iconic images, followed by hierarchical labeling of categories, instance spotting, and instance segmentation using Amazon Mechanical Turk.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Segmentations were not collected for 11 specific categories due to them having too many instances, being ambiguous/difficult to label, causing confusion with other categories, or having too few instances.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were primarily collected from Flickr, which contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords, as well as Google or Bing image search.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize duplicates across dataset splits.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: An explicit filtering stage was performed using an AMT task to remove invalid or iconic images from the candidate pool.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation pipeline consisted of three primary tasks: labeling the categories present in the image using a hierarchical approach, locating and marking all instances of the labeled categories, and segmenting each object instance.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon's Mechanical Turk (AMT) and a modified version of the OpenSurfaces project interface.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: An explicit verification step was performed on each segmented instance where 3 to 5 workers judged the segmentation quality. Segmentations of insufficient quality were discarded.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers for category labeling and instance spotting; 1 worker for instance segmentation; 3 to 5 workers for segmentation verification.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was split into two releases (2014 and 2015). The dataset will evolve and grow over time with up-to-date information available online.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Segmentations are missing for 11 categories. Also, for images with more than 10-15 instances of a category tightly grouped together, individual instances are not distinguished and are marked as 'crowds'.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing for object recognition, detection, and segmentation. Annotations for train and validation data are released, but not for test data.

name.evidence: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context

description.evidence: We introduce a new large-scale dataset that addresses three core research problems in scene understanding: detecting non-iconic views (or non-canonical perspectives [12]) of objects, contextual reasoning between objects and the precise 2D localization of objects.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: First and most importantly, we harvested a large set of images containing contextual relationships and non-iconic object views. We accomplished this using a surprisingly simple yet effective technique that queries for pairs of objects in conjunction with images retrieved via scene-based queries... Next, each image was labeled as containing particular object categories using a hierarchical labeling approach.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images... For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (AMT).

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: We did not collect segmentations for the following 11 categories: hat, shoe, eyeglasses (too many instances), mirror, window, door, street sign (ambiguous and difficult to label), plate, desk (due to confusion with bowl and dining table, respectively) and blender, hair brush (too few instances).

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: we collected images from Flickr which tends to have fewer iconic images. Flickr contains photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords... directly searching for specific categories using Google or Bing image search.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: We took care to minimize the chance of near-duplicate images existing across splits by explicitly removing near duplicates (detected with [43]) and grouping images by photographer and date taken.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: we searched for single categories and performed an explicit filtering stage to remove iconic images... We then created an AMT filtering task that allowed users to remove invalid or iconic images from a grid of 128 candidates

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Our annotation pipeline is split into 3 primary tasks: (a) labeling the categories present in the image... (b) locating and marking all instances of the labeled categories... and (c) segmenting each object instance.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: For all crowdsourcing tasks we used workers on Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (AMT)... For this stage we modified the excellent user interface developed by Bell et al. [16] for image segmentation.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: we also performed an explicit verification step on each segmented instance to ensure good quality. Multiple workers (3 to 5) were asked to judge each segmentation and indicate whether it matched the instance well or not. Segmentations of insufficient quality were discarded

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: To ensure high recall, 8 workers were asked to label each image... Each image was labeled by 8 workers... To minimize cost we only had a single worker segment each instance... Multiple workers (3 to 5) were asked to judge each segmentation

rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan.evidence: The first half of the dataset was released in 2014, the second half will be released in 2015... MS COCO will evolve and grow over time; up to date information is available online.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: we did not collect segmentations for the following 11 categories... After 10-15 instances of a category were segmented in an image, the remaining instances were marked as “crowds” using a single (possibly multipart) segment.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: The 2014 release contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images... Following established protocol, annotations for train and validation data will be released, but not for test.
